To hide means to put something — or yourself — in a place where others cannot see it or find it easily. The basic goal is always the same: to make something unavailable to view or discovery.

  • The cat hid under the bed.
  • She hid her diary inside her pillowcase.

"Hide" works in two directions:

1. You hide something (an object or person)
Here, you are the one doing the action, and something else is being concealed.

  • He hid the birthday gift in the closet.
  • The spy hid the documents inside a hollow book.
  • The mother hid her child during the storm.

2. You hide yourself
Here, you are both the one acting and the one being concealed. You remove yourself from sight.

  • The children hid behind the curtains.
  • The criminal hid in an abandoned warehouse.
  • When she heard the door open, she quickly hid.

"Hide" extends naturally to invisible, internal things — like emotions, thoughts, and reactions. When you hide a feeling, you have it inside but you don't show it to others.

  • He was terrified, but he hid his fear behind a calm smile.
  • She hid her disappointment and pretended to be happy for them.
  • It was obvious he was lying — he couldn't hide his guilt.
  • She tried to hide the fact that she had been crying.

This is one of the most common uses of "hide" in everyday English. Any time you feel something but deliberately don't let it show, you are hiding it.

You can also hide facts, information, or the truth — meaning you keep them from others so they don't know.

  • The company hid its losses from investors.
  • He hid the real reason for his resignation.
  • She had nothing to hide — her accounts were completely open.
  • The report hid the uncomfortable facts in a footnote nobody would read.

Notice that "hiding" information is almost always intentional. It implies a choice to keep something out of view.

"Hide" is an irregular verb — it doesn't follow the normal -ed pattern.

FormWordExample
Base formhideI always hide my keys in the same place.
Past simplehidShe hid the letter.
Past participlehiddenThe treasure was hidden for centuries.
Present participlehidingHe is hiding something from us.

(The past participle "hidden" is used with helping verbs like "has," "have," "had," "was," "were.")

  • The keys were hidden under the mat.
  • Someone has hidden my files.
  • I had hidden the spare key behind the plant.

Occasionally you'll see "hid" used informally as a past participle, but "hidden" is the correct standard form.

Hide away
To go somewhere private and secluded, often to be alone or to avoid people. Also means to put something in a very private, secret place.

  • After the argument, she hid away in her room for days.
  • He hid away his savings in a tin box under the floorboards.

Hide out
To stay in a secret location to avoid being found, usually because you are in danger or trouble.

  • The fugitive hid out in a cabin deep in the forest.
  • We hid out in the library until the rain passed.

Hide behind (something)
To use something as a shield or excuse to avoid accountability, responsibility, or the truth. This is almost always figurative.

  • She always hides behind humor when she feels vulnerable.
  • The politician hid behind legal language to avoid giving a straight answer.
  • Don't hide behind your work — face the problem directly.

Have nothing to hide
To be completely innocent, honest, or transparent — to have no secrets that would cause embarrassment or trouble.

  • "Check my phone if you want — I have nothing to hide."

Hidden agenda
A secret, concealed purpose behind what someone appears to be doing openly.

  • We started to doubt her motives — it seemed like she had a hidden agenda.

Hidden gem
Something (or someone) that is excellent, valuable, or special but not yet widely known.

  • That little restaurant on the side street is a real hidden gem.

In hiding
In a state of concealment — staying somewhere secret to avoid being found.

  • The dissident was in hiding for three years.

Hiding is usually intentional. When you say someone hid something, the natural assumption is that they chose to do so deliberately. If something is concealed by accident, English speakers more often say "it was buried under" or "it got lost in" rather than "hidden."

Hiding implies effort or purpose. You don't just place something somewhere — you specifically choose a place that makes it hard to see or find. A key left on a table isn't hidden; a key placed inside a hollowed-out book is.

Hidden vs. secret: Something "hidden" is physically placed out of sight. Something "secret" is kept from people's knowledge. The two overlap often, but they're not identical.

  • A secret can exist even without being physically hidden (a plan kept inside one's mind).
  • Something hidden might not be a secret at all — a birthday cake hidden in the kitchen is hidden but not exactly secret in a serious sense.

Conceal vs. hide: "Conceal" is more formal and is often used for deliberate, calculated hiding — especially of information, weapons, or intentions. "Hide" is the everyday, natural choice for most situations. They are frequently interchangeable, but "conceal" carries a slightly heavier, more serious tone.

  • She hid her feelings. (natural, everyday)
  • He concealed a weapon. (formal, serious)

"Hide" means to place something — physical or non-physical — out of sight and out of easy reach, either to protect it, to avoid discovery, or to prevent others from knowing. It works for objects, people, feelings, facts, and intentions. The one constant thread across all uses: something that exists is being deliberately kept from being seen or found.
